theme: Elihu’s case for God’s majesty, the storm approaches
readingInstruction: Read Job 35:1-37:24. Elihu continues with three more speeches. They get steadily more poetic, ending with a long description of a storm. Read chapter 37 as if you are watching a storm roll in, because the next chapter is the answer from the storm.
settingTheScene: Elihu’s last three speeches are the finest in his section. He starts with a charge that Job is claiming too much, but the speeches build toward a description of God’s majesty in nature. By the end, the sky is darkening and the thunder is rolling. There is a sense of something about to happen. In the next chapter, God will speak, and he will speak from the whirlwind.
observation: Elihu asks, “If you have sinned, what do you accomplish against him?” (35:6).
He says that people cry out under oppression but do not ask, “Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?” (35:10).
“Behold, God is mighty, and does not despise any; he is mighty in strength of understanding” (36:5).
“He delivers the afflicted by their affliction and opens their ear by oppression” (36:15).
“Behold, God is great, and we know him not; the number of his years is unsearchable” (36:26).
He describes rain, thunder, and lightning as the work of God (36:27-33).
“God thunders wondrously with his voice; he does great things that we cannot comprehend” (37:5).
He tells Job: “Stop and consider the wondrous works of God” (37:14).

The final line: “The Almighty, we cannot find him; he is great in power; justice and abundant righteousness he will not violate. Therefore men fear him; he does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit” (37:23-24).
interpretation:
Elihu’s best contribution is his emphasis on God as Maker. In 35:10 he asks a beautiful question: “Where is God my Maker, who gives songs in the night?” It points to something Job and his friends have all but forgotten: God is not only a judge. He is the one who gives songs in the dark. The God who allows the night is also the God who sings in it.

His description in chapter 36 of how God uses affliction deserves attention. “He delivers the afflicted by their affliction.” This is a rich line. God uses suffering to open ears, to teach people, and to bring them to himself. It is a true principle, and many believers can testify that they heard God most clearly in their pain. But Elihu is wrong if he thinks that this is the only reason suffering happens. In Job’s case, the real reason is not that.

The speech ends with weather. The thunderstorm in chapter 37 is a piece of poetry. Elihu says that God sends the snow and the rain, that he controls the clouds, and that no one can comprehend how it all works. “Do you know how God lays his command upon them?” (37:15). It is a series of questions, and it prepares for the greater questions to come. In a way, Elihu has started to do what God will do: use creation to remind a human being how small he is.

The last verse is a good summary. “He does not regard any who are wise in their own conceit.” It is a warning to Job and to Elihu himself. Elihu is also wise in his own conceit, as the book is about to reveal. All the human voices have spoken, and none of them has understood. Now there is silence, and then the storm.
connection: Psalm 42:8 says, “By day the LORD commands his steadfast love, and at night his song is with me.” Paul and Silas sang hymns in prison at midnight (Acts 16:25). Psalm 29 praises the voice of the LORD in the thunder. Jesus calmed a storm and made the disciples ask, “Who then is this?” (Mark 4:41).
application:
Pay attention to the weather this week. When there is a storm, watch it and pray Psalm 29. Let it remind you that you are small and God is great.

Ask God to give you a song in the night. If you are in a dark season, tell him that you are waiting for the song.

Be wary of any belief that explains everything about suffering. God is great, and we know him not.
prayerPrompts: Praise God for his greatness, in your own words.
Thank him for songs in the night.
Ask him to keep you from being wise in your own eyes.
